source: Wikipedia Electron affinity (data page): Ge 1.2326764(13) eV (Scheer et al. 1998); WebElements 119 kJ/mol
reason: The measured electron affinity of germanium is 1.233 eV. The value 1.35 is an outdated PubChem figure and is about 9.5% too high.

source: Wikipedia Electron affinity (data page): Rb 0.485916(21) eV; WebElements 46.9 kJ/mol
reason: The precisely measured electron affinity of rubidium is 0.4859 eV. The value 0.468 is about 3.7% low and looks like a transposed digit.

source: Wikipedia Electron affinity (data page): Sr 0.05206(6) eV (Andersen et al. 1997)
reason: Unlike Be and Mg, strontium forms a bound anion. Its electron affinity is well measured at 0.052 eV, so null is wrong.

source: CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights (ciaaw.org/abridged-atomic-weights.htm): Zr 91.222 ± 0.003 (2024 revision)
reason: In 2024 IUPAC/CIAAW revised zirconium's standard atomic weight from 91.224(2) to 91.222(3). The abridged value is now 91.222.

source: CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights: As 74.922 ± 0.001; full value 74.921595(6)
reason: This is not the abridged value, and it is also mis-rounded: 74.921595 rounds to 74.92160, not 74.92159. The IUPAC abridged value is 74.922.

source: CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights: Y 88.906 ± 0.001
reason: The dataset uses abridged values elsewhere (for example Rb 85.468). The IUPAC abridged value for yttrium is 88.906.

source: CIAAW abridged standard atomic weights: Se 78.971 ± 0.008
reason: The IUPAC abridged value is 78.971. The value 78.97 is a further-rounded version (as used by PubChem), not the abridged one.

source: Alvarez, Dalton Trans. 2013, 42, 8617 (as quoted by WebElements: Y 275 pm); Bondi gives no Y value
reason: Under the stated Bondi/Alvarez convention, yttrium's van der Waals radius is 275 pm. The value 219 pm is about 20% low and has no clear source.

source: Alvarez, Dalton Trans. 2013, 42, 8617 (as quoted by WebElements: Zr 252 pm); Bondi gives no Zr value
reason: Under the stated Bondi/Alvarez convention, zirconium's van der Waals radius is 252 pm. The value 186 pm is about 26% low.

source: Wikipedia Gallium infobox: a = 452.05 pm, b = 766.25 pm, c = 452.66 pm (20 °C); WebElements a=451.97, b=766.33, c=452.6 pm
reason: 766 pm is the b axis of alpha-Ga in the standard Cmce setting. The c axis is 452.7 pm, and the convention says cPm is c.

source: Wikipedia Bromine infobox: orthorhombic oS8, a = 674.30 pm, b = 466.85 pm, c = 870.02 pm (triple point)
reason: Solid bromine is orthorhombic with a well-known c axis of about 870 pm. The dataset fills cPm for other non-cubic solids (for example Ga), so null leaves out a known value.

source: Wikipedia Krypton infobox/NUBASE: 78Kr 0.36%, half-life 9.2×10^21 y, double electron capture (observed 2013, Gavrilyuk et al.)
reason: Kr-78 has been observed to decay by double electron capture. This dataset lists other observed double-beta emitters (Ge-76, Se-82, Zr-96) under radioactive, so Kr-78 should be moved there too.

current: Gallium melts just above room temperature but boils only above 2,400 °C, giving it one of the longest liquid ranges of any element. Gallium compounds power LEDs and fast electronics.
corrected: "Gallium melts just above room temperature but does not boil until about 2,400 °C, giving it one of the longest liquid ranges of any element. Gallium compounds power LEDs and fast electronics."
source: Entry's own boilingPoint 2673 K (= 2399.85 °C); Wikipedia/RSC 2400 °C; CRC Handbook 2229 °C; WebElements 2477 K
reason: Reputable values for gallium's boiling point run from about 2,200 °C to 2,400 °C, and the entry's own 2673 K is just below 2,400 °C. 'Boils only above 2,400 °C' therefore overstates it. 'About 2,400 °C' is accurate and keeps the point about its long liquid range.
